text: The last lesson said a subnet mask decides exactly where an IP address splits into network and host portions, but left the details for here. This lesson works through that split with real numbers, using CIDR notation — the shorthand you'll see everywhere in real network diagrams, cloud consoles, and firewall rules.

Northbridge Retail doesn't put every device on one flat network. It splits its address space into subnets: one for the warehouse floor, one for corporate office machines, one for guest Wi-Fi. That keeps broadcast traffic contained, lets different security rules apply to each group, and stops a problem on one subnet from flooding onto another.

CIDR notation writes the subnet mask as a slash and a number, like slash 24, and that number is simply how many of the address's 32 bits are the network portion. A slash 24 is common because it lines up neatly with octet boundaries, but CIDR can cut anywhere to create smaller subnets. The bits left over are host bits, and they determine the subnet's size — two to the power of the host bits, minus two, because the network address and the broadcast address are both reserved.

Northbridge's warehouse has about 40 devices today with room to grow to 55. A slash 27 is too small at 30 usable hosts. A slash 26 gives 62 usable hosts — plenty of room without the waste of a full slash 24. So the warehouse gets 192.168.10.0 slash 26: network address .0, usable hosts .1 through .62, broadcast address .63.
Next up, lesson nine: switching and routing basics, where these addresses actually get used to move traffic.
